title: Control of Breathing, Altitude and Diving

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: In a resting adult at sea level the breathing controller's set point is an arterial PCO2 of about {{c1::40}} mmHg, with pH about 7.40.
cards.quote: arterial PCO2 about 40 mmHg and pH about 7.40 at rest
cards.section: The loop: a sensor, a set point, a lever

cards.front: In the breathing control loop, what is minute ventilation, and roughly how large is it in a resting adult?
cards.back: Tidal volume times breathing frequency, about 6 L/min at rest, of which about 4.2 L/min reaches the alveoli.
cards.quote: tidal volume times breathing frequency, about 6 L/min in a resting adult, of which about 4.2 L/min reaches the alveoli
cards.section: The loop: a sensor, a set point, a lever

cards.front: "Control of breathing" hides two separate questions. What are they, and what answers each?
cards.back: Where the alternation of inspiration and expiration comes from (the rhythm, from the ventral respiratory column) and what sets how hard that rhythm drives the muscles (the drive, set largely by the chemoreflexes at rest).
cards.quote: where the alternation of inspiration and expiration comes from (the rhythm), and what sets how hard it drives the muscles (the drive)
cards.section: The loop: a sensor, a set point, a lever

cards.front: In the breathing chemoreflex, a curve turns a gas error into a change in ventilation, and a curve's steepness is its {{c1::gain}}.
cards.quote: each turning a gas error into a change in ventilation; a curve's steepness is its gain
cards.section: The loop: a sensor, a set point, a lever

cards.front: For a fixed carbon dioxide production, alveolar PCO2 is {{c1::inversely}} proportional to alveolar ventilation.
cards.quote: Alveolar PCO2 is inversely proportional to alveolar ventilation, for a fixed carbon dioxide production.
cards.section: Why carbon dioxide runs the loop

cards.front: Simplified alveolar gas equation: alveolar PO2 = 0.21 x (barometric pressure - 47) - {{c1::alveolar PCO2 / R}}.
cards.back: 0.21 is the inspired oxygen fraction, 47 mmHg is saturated water vapour pressure, and R, the respiratory exchange ratio, is 0.80.
cards.quote: alveolar PO2 = 0.21 x (barometric pressure - 47) - alveolar PCO2 / R
cards.section: Why carbon dioxide runs the loop

cards.front: A resting adult breathes air at a barometric pressure of 760 mmHg with arterial PCO2 at 40 mmHg. Water vapour is 47 mmHg and R is 0.80. Give the alveolar PO2 from the simplified alveolar gas equation.
cards.back: About 100 mmHg. Humidified inspired oxygen is 0.21 x (760 - 47) = 149.7 mmHg; the carbon dioxide term is 40/0.80 = 50.0 mmHg; 149.7 - 50.0 = 99.7 mmHg.
cards.section: Why carbon dioxide runs the loop

cards.front: A resting adult at sea level doubles alveolar ventilation, from about 4.2 to 8.4 L/min. What happens to arterial PCO2 and to pH?
cards.back: Carbon dioxide halves, from about 40 to about 20 mmHg, and pH climbs from 7.40 to roughly 7.6: a severe respiratory alkalosis.
cards.why: Halving carbon dioxide is worth about 0.3 pH units because pH goes as the logarithm of the ratio, and log 2 is 0.3.
cards.quote: Carbon dioxide halves, from about 40 to about 20 mmHg, and pH climbs from 7.40 to roughly 7.6, a severe respiratory alkalosis.
cards.section: Why carbon dioxide runs the loop

cards.front: The same resting adult doubles alveolar ventilation at sea level. What happens to alveolar PO2 and to the oxygen content of the blood, and why do the two answers differ so much?
cards.back: Alveolar PO2 rises from about 100 to about 125 mmHg, but saturation moves only from about 97 to about 98.5 percent and content rises by about 1.5 percent, because hemoglobin was already nearly full (model values).
cards.quote: hemoglobin was already about 97 percent full, so saturation moves only to about 98.5 percent and oxygen content rises by about 1.5 percent
cards.section: Why carbon dioxide runs the loop

cards.front: Even at the lever's ceiling, with arterial PCO2 driven to zero at sea level, how much more oxygen can extra ventilation add to the blood?
cards.back: Only about 2.5 percent more content; alveolar PO2 can reach at most the inspired 149.7 mmHg, and hemoglobin is already nearly saturated (model values).
cards.quote: (PCO2 at zero, alveolar PO2 equal to the 149.7 mmHg inspired) content rises only about 2.5 percent
cards.section: Why carbon dioxide runs the loop

cards.front: State the central idea of the breathing lesson: which gas does the loop control, and why that one?
cards.back: Breathing is a feedback loop that controls the gas its lever can move. Near the resting point a change in ventilation moves PCO2 and pH a great deal and oxygen content almost not at all, so gain is high for carbon dioxide and nearly zero for oxygen.
cards.quote: Breathing is a feedback loop that controls the gas its lever can move.
cards.section: Why carbon dioxide runs the loop

cards.front: Below roughly what alveolar PO2 does the oxygen arm of the breathing controller start to matter, and what makes that region different?
cards.back: Below an alveolar PO2 of about 60 mmHg, which is the steep part of both the chemoreflex curve and the hemoglobin curve, so extra ventilation there buys real oxygen content.
cards.quote: below an alveolar PO2 of about 60 mmHg, on the steep part of both the chemoreflex curve and the hemoglobin curve
cards.section: Why carbon dioxide runs the loop

cards.front: A resting adult at sea level halves alveolar ventilation instead of doubling it. What happens to alveolar PCO2, alveolar PO2 and oxygen content, and what does that show about the "ventilation does nothing for oxygen" rule?
cards.back: Alveolar PCO2 doubles to about 80 mmHg, alveolar PO2 falls to about 50, saturation to about 85 percent and content by about 13 percent. The rule is about gain near the resting point, not about large hypoventilation, which is a serious oxygen problem even at sea level. (Model values, arterial taken as alveolar.)
cards.quote: large hypoventilation is a serious oxygen problem even at sea level. The rule is about gain near the operating point.
cards.section: Why carbon dioxide runs the loop

cards.front: In the alveolar gas equation, how far does alveolar PO2 move for every 1 mmHg of arterial PCO2 the controller allows, and what does that imply about a carbon dioxide controller?
cards.back: 1.25 mmHg, which is 1/R. So a loop holding PCO2 within a couple of mmHg of 40 also holds alveolar PO2 within a few mmHg of 100: the carbon dioxide controller is an oxygen controller by proxy.
cards.quote: The carbon dioxide controller is an oxygen controller by proxy
cards.section: Why carbon dioxide runs the loop

cards.front: Under what two kinds of condition does a carbon-dioxide-only controller stop guaranteeing arterial oxygen, so that a dedicated oxygen arm is needed?
cards.back: At altitude, where inspired PO2 falls, and in lung disease where shunt or ventilation-perfusion mismatch lowers arterial PO2 at a normal PCO2. The proxy holds only while gas exchange is intact enough for the alveolar gas equation to predict arterial oxygen.
cards.quote: in lung disease where shunt or ventilation-perfusion mismatch lowers arterial PO2 at a normal PCO2
cards.section: Why carbon dioxide runs the loop

cards.front: Why can the brain sample arterial carbon dioxide directly, and what signal do central chemoreceptors actually read?
cards.back: Carbon dioxide is lipid-soluble and crosses the blood-brain barrier readily; once in brain extracellular fluid and cerebrospinal fluid it is hydrated and releases hydrogen ions, and it is sensed primarily as those hydrogen ion changes.
cards.quote: Carbon dioxide is lipid-soluble and crosses the blood-brain barrier readily, so the brain can sample it where it sits.
cards.section: Carbon dioxide is sensed as hydrogen ions, inside the brain

cards.front: Why is a controller tuned to carbon dioxide also a controller of acid-base status?
cards.back: Ventilation sets arterial PCO2, and arterial PCO2 is one of the two terms that set pH.
cards.quote: ventilation sets arterial PCO2, and arterial PCO2 is one of the two terms that set pH
cards.section: Carbon dioxide is sensed as hydrogen ions, inside the brain

cards.front: Name the main central chemoreceptor population of the medulla and the two proton-sensing molecules identified in its neurons in mice.
cards.back: The retrotrapezoid nucleus, a small population on the ventral medullary surface, proton-sensitive through the potassium channel TASK-2 and the proton-activated receptor GPR4.
cards.quote: proton-sensitive through the potassium channel TASK-2 and the proton-activated receptor GPR4
cards.section: Carbon dioxide is sensed as hydrogen ions, inside the brain

cards.front: In rat and mouse networks, where do retrotrapezoid nucleus neurons project, and what does that pathway accomplish?
cards.back: To the pre-Botzinger complex, the nucleus tractus solitarius and pontine nuclei: the route from a pH signal to a bigger breath.
cards.quote: they project to the pre-Botzinger complex, the nucleus tractus solitarius and pontine nuclei, the route from a pH signal to a bigger breath
cards.section: Carbon dioxide is sensed as hydrogen ions, inside the brain

cards.front: A study shows that astrocytes in the medulla are acid-sensitive and that stimulating them changes breathing. Why does the lesson treat that as weaker than identifying a central chemoreceptor?
cards.back: Because showing that a cell is acid-sensitive and that manipulating it changes breathing is weaker than showing it is the sensor; as of a 2023 review, several proposed central chemoreceptor cell types had not met every criterion.
cards.quote: Showing that a cell is acid-sensitive and that manipulating it changes breathing is weaker than showing it is the sensor.
cards.section: Carbon dioxide is sensed as hydrogen ions, inside the brain

cards.front: Where does the peripheral oxygen sensor sit, and what two features let it respond within seconds?
cards.back: The carotid body at the fork of each carotid artery. It is small and heavily perfused, so it reads arterial blood before the tissues take any oxygen out.
cards.quote: small, heavily perfused, and for that reason able to respond within seconds
cards.section: The carotid body is the oxygen sensor, and it is fast

cards.front: In the carotid body, which cells transduce hypoxia, and in which nerve do their afferents run? What is the aortic equivalent?
cards.back: Glomus cells depolarize in hypoxia and release transmitter onto afferents in the carotid sinus branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve. Aortic bodies contribute too, with oxygen-sensing afferents in the vagus.
cards.quote: Aortic bodies contribute too, with oxygen-sensing afferents in the vagus.
cards.section: The carotid body is the oxygen sensor, and it is fast

cards.front: Two structures sit at the same carotid bifurcation. Distinguish the carotid body from the carotid sinus by organ type and stimulus.
cards.back: The carotid body is a chemoreceptor for arterial oxygen (also carbon dioxide and pH). The carotid sinus is a stretch-sensitive widening of the arterial wall, a baroreceptor for pressure. Same bifurcation, different organ and stimulus.
cards.quote: Same bifurcation, same nerve, different organ and stimulus.
cards.section: The carotid body is the oxygen sensor, and it is fast

cards.front: A patient has had both carotid bodies removed. Per the human denervation literature, what happens to the ventilatory response to hypoxia at a clamped normal PCO2, and to the response to hypercapnia?
cards.back: The normocapnic ventilatory response to hypoxia is permanently abolished in the patients reviewed, and the response to hypercapnia is reduced: the organ carries the oxygen arm and part of the carbon dioxide arm.
cards.quote: permanently abolishes the normocapnic ventilatory response to hypoxia in the patients reviewed, and reduces the response to hypercapnia
cards.section: The carotid body is the oxygen sensor, and it is fast

cards.front: Epas1 (HIF-2alpha) was deleted embryonically in mouse catecholaminergic tissue. Give the three results in the adults, including the isoform control.
cards.back: Virtually no tyrosine hydroxylase-positive glomus cells; a substantially reduced hypoxic ventilatory response; a retained response to inspired carbon dioxide. The matching HIF-1alpha deletion kept its hypoxic response.
cards.quote: adult animals had virtually no tyrosine hydroxylase-positive glomus cells and a substantially reduced hypoxic ventilatory response
cards.section: The carotid body is the oxygen sensor, and it is fast

cards.front: On a human ventilatory response curve against arterial PCO2, what shape is the relation, and roughly what slope is representative in awake adults?
cards.back: Increasing and approximately linear over a broad range, of the order of 2 to 5 L/min per mmHg by rebreathing, with 2 taken as the conservative figure.
cards.why: Reported slopes depend on the protocol, rebreathing or steady state, and on the subject, so this is an order of magnitude rather than a value to quote.
cards.quote: a representative slope is of the order of 2 to 5 L/min per mmHg by rebreathing, with 2 taken here as the conservative figure
cards.section: Reading the response curves: two gains

cards.front: Taking the carbon dioxide response slope as 2 L/min per mmHg and resting ventilation as about 6 L/min, how much extra ventilation does a PCO2 that drifts 1 mmHg high call for, as a fraction of resting breathing?
cards.back: About 2 L/min, which is about a third more ventilation than the resting 6 L/min.
cards.quote: a PCO2 that drifts 1 mmHg high calls for about a third more ventilation
cards.section: Reading the response curves: two gains

cards.front: Why must a carbon dioxide response curve be reported with its oxygen condition stated?
cards.back: Because the slope depends on the prevailing PO2, being steeper at low PO2.
cards.quote: The slope also depends on the prevailing PO2, being steeper at low PO2
cards.section: Reading the response curves: two gains

cards.front: Against alveolar PO2, what shape does the human ventilatory response take, and over what range does it steepen?
cards.back: Not a line: shallow above about 60 mmHg, steepening as alveolar PO2 enters roughly 50 to 60 mmHg in Weil and colleagues' normal subjects, who fitted a hyperbola with ventilation rising as 1/(PO2 - 32).
cards.quote: It is shallow above about 60 mmHg and steepens as alveolar PO2 enters roughly 50 to 60 mmHg
cards.section: Reading the response curves: two gains

cards.front: In the fitted hyperbola for the hypoxic ventilatory response, slope goes as 1/(PO2 - 32) squared. Compute the ratio of the slope at an alveolar PO2 of 50 mmHg to that at 100 mmHg, and say why the ratio is individual-independent.
cards.back: (100 - 32)squared / (50 - 32)squared = (68/18)squared, about 14. The ratio is fixed within the fitted form because the shape parameter cancels; the absolute slope does depend on it.
cards.section: Reading the response curves: two gains

cards.front: Given that the hypoxic response steepens about 14-fold between alveolar PO2 100 and 50 mmHg, why is resting breathing still run by carbon dioxide?
cards.back: The oxygen sensor is not weak; it is in the wrong place on its own axis. At rest the operating point sits at about 100 mmHg, on the shallow part of the curve.
cards.quote: The oxygen sensor is not weak. It is in the wrong place on its own axis.
cards.section: Reading the response curves: two gains

cards.front: At rest at sea level each gas drifts 5 mmHg from its resting value (PCO2 40, PO2 100 mmHg). Which error does the controller correct, and which does it almost ignore?
cards.back: The carbon dioxide error, by a wide margin: at 2 L/min per mmHg, 5 mmHg calls for about 10 L/min of extra ventilation, more than doubling resting breathing. The same 5 mmHg of PO2 is worth about 0.1 to 0.3 L/min.
cards.why: That is a slope roughly thirty to ninety times shallower, depending on the sensitivity assumed.
cards.quote: The carbon dioxide error, by a wide margin.
cards.section: Reading the response curves: two gains

cards.front: At rest at sea level, is the oxygen arm of the chemoreflex silent? State what it does and does not contribute.
cards.back: It is on and reporting, and its tonic traffic contributes to resting drive and to part of the carbon dioxide response. What is worth almost nothing is its answer to a few mmHg of PO2 near 100.
cards.quote: At rest the oxygen arm is on and reporting, and its tonic traffic does contribute to resting drive
cards.section: Reading the response curves: two gains

cards.front: Why must a hypoxic ventilatory response curve be measured under isocapnia, and what does an unclamped recording get wrong?
cards.back: Unclamped, breathing harder lowers PCO2, and that hypocapnia restrains ventilation through its alkalosis at the medullary chemoreceptors and the carotid body. Drive and brake interact, so the uncontrolled reading understates the oxygen drive.
cards.quote: the harder the subject breathes, the harder the brake pulls, so the uncontrolled reading understates the oxygen drive itself
cards.section: Reading the response curves: two gains

cards.front: Volunteers breathe gas of falling oxygen fraction. In protocol A carbon dioxide is added to hold alveolar PCO2 at its resting value; in protocol B it is allowed to fall. At an alveolar PO2 of 50 mmHg, which protocol records the higher ventilation, and why?
cards.back: Protocol A. In B the falling PCO2 adds an opposing alkalotic brake acting both centrally and at the carotid body; clamping PCO2 removes that restraint, so the clamped run reads higher at the same oxygen tension.
cards.quote: carbon dioxide was added to the inspired gas to hold alveolar PCO2 at its resting value, so ventilation could be plotted against oxygen alone
cards.section: Reading the response curves: two gains

cards.front: Where in the brainstem does the breathing rhythm arise, and which oscillator generates inspiration against which one for active expiration?
cards.back: In the ventral respiratory column of the medulla: the pre-Botzinger complex generates inspiration, while a parafacial oscillator near the retrotrapezoid nucleus is implicated in active expiration.
cards.quote: the pre-Botzinger complex generates inspiration, while a parafacial oscillator near the retrotrapezoid nucleus is implicated in active expiration
cards.section: The clock: the rhythm is made in the medulla

cards.front: In the ventral respiratory column, what do the rostral and caudal ventral respiratory groups contain?
cards.back: Inspiratory and expiratory premotor neurons respectively, which relay drive onward to the motor neurons.
cards.quote: contain inspiratory and expiratory premotor neurons respectively, which relay drive onward to the motor neurons
cards.section: The clock: the rhythm is made in the medulla

cards.front: A neonatal rat brainstem and spinal cord are kept working in a dish with no lungs and no blood. Describe the three results that located the inspiratory rhythm generator.
cards.back: The rhythm survived removal of tissue on either side of one small ventrolateral region, stopped when that region came out, and continued in thin slices containing it: the pre-Botzinger complex.
cards.quote: The rhythm survived removal of tissue on either side of one small ventrolateral region, stopped when that region came out, and continued in thin slices containing it.
cards.section: The clock: the rhythm is made in the medulla

cards.front: The in vitro neonatal rat work showed the pre-Botzinger complex is necessary locally and that a slice containing it suffices. Name two claims that result does not establish.
cards.back: It does not establish the adult human circuit, nor that one intrinsic pacemaker mechanism accounts for every breath.
cards.quote: It does not establish the adult human circuit, nor that one intrinsic pacemaker mechanism accounts for every breath.
cards.section: The clock: the rhythm is made in the medulla

cards.front: At terrestrial altitude, which term of the inspired gas falls and which stays put, and what does that do to the loop's operating point?
cards.back: The inspired oxygen fraction stays at 0.21; barometric pressure falls, and with it the partial pressure of oxygen in every breath. The loop is unchanged but its operating point moves onto the part of the oxygen curve where the lever has authority.
cards.quote: At terrestrial altitude the inspired oxygen fraction stays at 0.21; what falls is barometric pressure
cards.section: Altitude: the same lever, in a better place

cards.front: Model values: barometric pressure 500 mmHg, inspired oxygen fraction 0.21, water vapour 47 mmHg, R 0.80, steady state. Give alveolar PO2 at an arterial PCO2 of 40 mmHg, then after hypoxic hyperventilation lowers it to 30 mmHg, then the gain.
cards.back: Humidified inspired oxygen is 0.21 x 453 = 95.1 mmHg. At PCO2 40: 95.1 - 50.0 = 45.1 mmHg. At PCO2 30: 95.1 - 37.5 = 57.6 mmHg. Gain 12.5 mmHg, checked as (40 - 30)/0.80.
cards.quote: Independent check: (40 - 30)/0.80 = 12.5 mmHg.
cards.section: Altitude: the same lever, in a better place

cards.front: A volunteer is in a steady state at barometric pressure 450 mmHg, inspired oxygen fraction 0.21, water vapour 47 mmHg, R 0.80, arterial PCO2 measured at 32 mmHg. Give the alveolar PO2.
cards.back: About 45 mmHg. Humidified inspired oxygen is 0.21 x (450 - 47) = 84.6 mmHg; the carbon dioxide term is 32/0.80 = 40.0 mmHg; 84.6 - 40.0 = 44.6 mmHg.
cards.quote: inspired oxygen fraction 0.21, water vapour 47 mmHg, R 0.80, negligible inspired carbon dioxide, steady state
cards.section: Altitude: the same lever, in a better place

cards.front: The altitude worked problem yields 12.5 mmHg. Two cautions attach to that figure: what are they?
cards.back: It is alveolar PO2, not arterial, since arterial PO2 needs gas-exchange information the calculation lacks; and 12.5 mmHg is the model's output, not a measured acclimatization benefit.
cards.quote: 12.5 mmHg is the model's output, not a measured acclimatization benefit
cards.section: Altitude: the same lever, in a better place

cards.front: The identical 10 mmHg of carbon dioxide washout buys 12.5 mmHg of alveolar PO2 at sea level and at a barometric pressure of 500 mmHg alike. Which setting turns that into more oxygen carried in the blood, and by roughly how much?
cards.back: At 500 mmHg, by roughly tenfold. At sea level 12.5 mmHg moves alveolar PO2 from about 100 to 112 mmHg on the flat top of the hemoglobin curve, raising content about 1 percent; at 500 mmHg the same push lands on the steep part and content rises about 10 percent.
cards.why: Model values, read off alveolar PO2 and ignoring the leftward curve shift the alkalosis causes, so an upper bound.
cards.quote: Same lever, same push, about ten times the oxygen
cards.section: Altitude: the same lever, in a better place

cards.front: A lowlander ascends rapidly to high altitude. Give the direction and time course for arterial PCO2, arterial pH and plasma bicarbonate, and say how the pH change acts on ventilation.
cards.back: PCO2 down and pH up over minutes to hours; plasma bicarbonate falls over days as the kidney increases bicarbonate excretion, partly correcting the alkalosis. The alkalosis inhibits ventilation centrally and at the carotid body, holding it below what hypoxia alone would drive.
cards.quote: the alkalosis inhibits ventilation centrally and at the carotid body, holding it below what hypoxia alone would drive
cards.section: Altitude: the same lever, in a better place

cards.front: Days into an altitude stay, cerebrospinal fluid pH may still be alkaline, yet ventilation rises further. Which change in the loop allows that?
cards.back: Carotid body sensitivity and central sensitization rise over days, so ventilation can rise further even where cerebrospinal fluid pH stays alkaline.
cards.quote: up, so ventilation can rise further even where cerebrospinal fluid pH stays alkaline
cards.section: Altitude: the same lever, in a better place

cards.front: In lowlanders ascending to 5160 m over ten days, a derived index of renal compensation plateaued after about five days. How should that five-day figure be read?
cards.back: As a protocol-specific trajectory, not a universal deadline: the renal clock has been measured in lowlanders, but only under that ascent protocol.
cards.quote: The renal clock has been measured in lowlanders, but as a protocol-specific trajectory rather than a universal deadline
cards.section: Altitude: the same lever, in a better place

cards.front: How does acute mountain sickness commonly present after rapid ascent in a non-acclimatized person, and what does the feedback loop explain about it?
cards.back: Commonly as headache, accompanied variably by appetite loss, nausea, fatigue or dizziness. A cerebral mechanism for uncomplicated cases is not settled: the loop gives the directions of the variables, not the headache.
cards.quote: the syndrome commonly presents as headache accompanied variably by appetite loss, nausea, fatigue or dizziness
cards.section: Altitude: the same lever, in a better place

cards.front: During a voluntary breath-hold, what mainly drives the urge to breathe, and why is the apnea break point a different matter?
cards.back: The urge tracks carbon dioxide in the main. The break point is influenced by both gases and no simple blood-gas rule fully explains it, because their relative weight varies with the starting gases, the lung volume and the person.
cards.quote: no simple blood-gas rule fully explains it, because their relative weight varies with the starting gases, the lung volume and the person
cards.section: Diving: the loop with the lever taken away

cards.front: What are the two autonomic limbs of the mammalian diving response during apnea?
cards.back: Parasympathetically mediated bradycardia together with sympathetically mediated peripheral vasoconstriction.
cards.quote: parasympathetically mediated bradycardia during apnea together with sympathetically mediated peripheral vasoconstriction
cards.section: Diving: the loop with the lever taken away

cards.front: Volunteers hold maximal prone apneas with cold face immersion, once after normal breathing and once after 15 seconds of hyperventilation. Predict the effect on hold length, on the saturation nadir, and on the diving response itself.
cards.back: Longer holds, by about 22 seconds on average, because the lower starting carbon dioxide delays the urge to breathe; a lower saturation nadir, by about 3 percentage points; and no stronger diving response.
cards.why: Hyperventilation moved the timer far more than it moved the supply, since the extra breathing added little to hemoglobin already nearly saturated.
cards.quote: Hyperventilation moved the timer far more than it moved the supply.
cards.section: Diving: the loop with the lever taken away

cards.front: Pre-apnea hyperventilation lengthens a breath-hold and lowers the saturation nadir. What hazard does that combination create, and what did the study not measure?
cards.back: Breath-holding may continue until extreme hypoxia produces blackout, since the timer is moved further than the supply. No blackout rate was measured in that protocol.
cards.quote: pre-dive hyperventilation may permit breath-holding to continue until extreme hypoxia produces blackout
cards.section: Diving: the loop with the lever taken away

cards.front: In the breath-hold study, finger pulse oximetry gave the saturation nadir. What does that measurement report, and what does it not?
cards.back: It reports peripheral hemoglobin saturation, not brain oxygenation.
cards.quote: Finger pulse oximetry reports peripheral hemoglobin saturation, not brain oxygenation.
cards.section: The breath-hold study

cards.front: Could the longer breath-hold after hyperventilation be explained simply by the extra oxygen stored? State what the store estimate gives and why it cannot settle the question.
cards.back: Lowering alveolar PCO2 from 40 to 17.4 mmHg adds about 120 mL of oxygen to the lungs and 17 mL to the blood, roughly half a minute of resting consumption, or about 70 mL from the study's own 29.0 mmHg control. The sum is too sensitive to starting gases, consumption during apnea, the alkalotic curve shift and cardiovascular redistribution: an order-of-magnitude bound, not a result.
cards.quote: an order-of-magnitude bound, not a result
cards.section: The breath-hold study

cards.front: A colleague concludes from the embryonic Epas1 deletion that HIF-2alpha is the acute oxygen sensor of the glomus cell. Name the design flaw and the two changes that would test the acute claim.
cards.back: A cell that is absent cannot report a sensing defect. Use an inducible or adult-onset deletion applied after the carotid body has formed, with glomus-cell number counted in the same animals tested; and a readout that does not sum the whole reflex, such as glomus-cell calcium or catecholamine secretion in slices, or carotid sinus nerve recording.
cards.quote: a cell that is absent cannot report a sensing defect
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In the glomus-cell knockout experiments, tyrosine hydroxylase-Cre is the driver. Why is that a confound, and what experiment complements it?
cards.back: The driver is also active in adrenal chromaffin cells and brainstem catecholaminergic groups, so a deficit could arise outside the carotid body. Carotid body-targeted re-expression is the complement.
cards.quote: so a deficit could arise outside the carotid body; carotid body-targeted re-expression is the complement
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In the adult-onset glomus-cell deletion, state in advance what each of the two outcomes would mean.
cards.back: If the cells are spared and the hypoxic response holds, that supports a mainly developmental role under the conditions tested, once deletion efficiency, timing and compensation are checked. If normally numbered cells show an acute deficit, the sensing claim survives.
cards.quote: If normally numbered cells show an acute deficit, the sensing claim survives.
cards.section: Design problem
